questions.prompt: How many lead statuses describe everything in your Book?

options.text: Four, the ones you actively work each day
Nine, and every lead sits in exactly one
Six, from New through to Customer
Seven, with Unqualified and Dead as tags

questions.prompt: What does a Recycled status tell you about a lead?

options.text: It came out of nurture and can be worked again
It was reassigned to you from another SDR's Book
It came back to you after a demo no-show
It was re-imported into HubSpot with fresh data

questions.source: Day 3, "The four statuses you actively work"

questions.prompt: A lead in your Book shows Opportunity. What does that mean?

options.text: You had a good call and plan to book this week
A demo is on the calendar but hasn't happened
The prospect asked for pricing, so it's warm
The AE marked it SQL and it's tied to a deal

questions.prompt: What puts a lead in Attempting?

options.text: It's been pre-vetted and given an AF1 or AF2 code
You connected with someone but haven't booked yet
It has a last contacted date within the last 30 days
It's on a call list you built for this week

questions.source: Day 3, "The four statuses you actively work"

questions.prompt: An Attempting account just landed in your Book. The status looks routine. What do you check before you dial?

options.text: Their Google reviews, for something to personalize
The activity history, for any past conversations
Their Instagram, to see how active the studio is
The record's create date, to see how old it is

questions.reveal: Someone may have had a real conversation with this account months ago. Calling cold and repeating a pitch they already turned down is how you burn an account.

questions.prompt: A lead in your Book shows Customer. On an old call, the owner mentioned opening a second location. What do you do?

options.text: Leave it, since customers aren't SDR prospects
Call to book a demo for the new location
Enroll her in a sequence about multi-location
Code it AFH so it sits at the top of tomorrow

questions.source: Handbook, Lead Statuses & Activity Clock; Day 3, "Not every lead deserves attention today"

questions.prompt: A teammate says Nurture leads are dead ends, so he never looks at them. What's the best response?

options.text: He's right, since Nurture means they said no for good
Nurture leads should get a call each month to stay warm
Nurture only matters for leads in Priority 1 verticals
Nurture was "not now," not "no," and it comes back Recycled

questions.source: Day 3, "Needs attention now vs. worked later"

questions.prompt: A rep says: "I own 2,000 leads, so I need to get through 2,000 dials." What's the best coaching?

options.text: Right, rotate through every lead before repeating any
Start with Nurture, since those leads already know us
Only New, Recycled and Attempting are live, so start there
Split dials evenly across all nine statuses each week

questions.source: Day 3, "Not every lead deserves attention today"

options.text: It moves to Unqualified
It moves to Nurture
It goes back to New
It's unassigned from you

questions.source: Day 3, "Where every lead ends up"; handbook, Lead Statuses & Activity Clock

questions.prompt: Which of these resets the 30-day activity clock?

options.text: A text you sent through HubSpot
A marketing email the owner opened
A LinkedIn profile view you made
A visit from the owner to our website

questions.prompt: How long does Nurture last before a lead becomes Recycled?

options.text: 30 days
Six weeks
Six months
Three months

questions.prompt: You log "Meeting Set" on a call. What happens to the lead's status?

options.text: Nothing until the AE accepts it
It moves straight to Opportunity
It moves to Booked on its own
You change it to Booked by hand

questions.prompt: You find a great Pilates studio on Google. You search HubSpot and nobody owns it. What's your next step?

options.text: Call today, then log it so the record is yours
Ask your manager to assign it before any outreach
Create the record and enroll it in a sequence
Ask your team in Slack if anyone minds you taking it

questions.prompt: You find a studio owned by another SDR. Nobody has touched it in five months. What do you do?

options.text: Leave it, because an inactive owned record isn't unowned
Work it, because five quiet months makes it fair game
Email the owner first, then claim it if she replies
Log one call on it so the record shows it's yours

questions.reveal: Never prospect into another SDR's Book. Inactivity only comes into an ownership decision when a genuine duplicate turns up, and a manager makes that call.

questions.prompt: You booked a demo for Friday. Then you find a duplicate record owned by another SDR. What happens?

options.text: You cancel the demo until ownership is settled
You hand the demo over to the other SDR to run
You merge the records yourself so the demo stays yours
You keep the meeting on track while a manager decides

questions.reveal: Outreach pauses on a disputed account, but an already-booked meeting doesn't. The booking SDR keeps it on track, and the manager approves ownership.

questions.prompt: The front desk manager says: "Take me off your list." You haven't spoken to the owner yet. What's right?

options.text: Treat the whole business as off-limits from now on
Wait three months, then try the front desk again
Mark that contact; the owner is still workable
Mark the company Dead so nobody calls it again

questions.reveal: A person-specific request applies to that person. Only an explicit request to stop contacting the whole business closes the company, and then you never go around it through someone else.
questions.source: Handbook, HubSpot Hygiene (Contact-Level Dead vs Company-Wide Restriction)

questions.prompt: You sit down with a full Book and a dozen things you could do. There's no priority score. What decides what you work first today?

options.text: Whichever list booked the most meetings last week
The daily order, then status and code set who's first
The call list your manager sends each morning
The newest leads in your Book, since they're freshest

questions.reveal: Start from the same order every day, then let status and code rank the accounts. A lead about to hit 30 days, or a callback you promised, outranks a fresh lead that can wait a day. Busy isn't the same as important.

questions.prompt: About how many cleaned leads should you bring into your Book?

options.text: About 25 a day, roughly 100 a week
About 10 a day, roughly 50 a week
About 50 a day, roughly 250 a week
Whatever your manager assigns you

questions.prompt: Which of these do you dial first today?

options.text: AFH, owner asked you to call back next week
AF1, pre-vetted yesterday, never dialed
AF2, Recycled, said they'd just switched last time
Attempting, no code, last touched 28 days ago

questions.reveal: The quiet Attempting lead drops to Nurture in two days. If nobody touches it today, it leaves your working pool for three months. The most urgent account is often the one that feels least exciting.

questions.prompt: Which of these do you leave alone today?

options.text: Recycled AF2, renewed elsewhere last time
Attempting, three no-answers in two weeks
Nurture, said not interested 5 weeks ago
New AF1, pre-vetted, never dialed

questions.prompt: Your next account is Recycled AF2. Notes say the owner said "we just switched software" last time. What do you do?

options.text: Dial right away, since Recycled means a fresh start
Plan an opener that acknowledges it, then dial
Skip it, since a past no means another no
Email first so the call doesn't catch her off guard

questions.source: Day 3, "What would you work first?" (account E)

questions.prompt: Your activity looks great, but your call lists get thinner every week. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: You're not replacing the leads that leave your Book
You're dialing at the wrong time of day
Your opener isn't turning connects into meetings
You're spending too long pre-vetting each lead

questions.prompt: A rep found a Pilates list that converts well and has worked only that list for three weeks. What's the risk?

options.text: None, since you work what converts until it stops
The list gets flagged as a duplicate in HubSpot
The AEs end up with too many Pilates demos
New and Recycled go untouched and the Book stalls

questions.reveal: One list always runs dry eventually. While you're working it, New and Recycled sit untouched and Attempting leads slip into Nurture. When the good list stops converting, there's nothing pre-vetted behind it, and your meetings drop for weeks while you rebuild. A diversified pipeline keeps meetings coming in a slow week.
questions.source: Day 3, "Not every lead deserves attention today" and "A Book is never finished"

questions.prompt: You chose "call first" this morning and dialed until 2 pm. What do you still owe before the day ends?

options.text: Nothing, since you've cleared the dial floor
A written recap of the day for your manager
Pre-vetting, the half you skipped this morning
A new static list ready for tomorrow

questions.prompt: Where do your codes go so HubSpot can pull them into a list?

options.text: The Lead Status field
SDR Additional Notes
A task on the record
The activity timeline

questions.prompt: What makes a lead AFH?

options.text: Timing: they're in market or asked for a callback
Fit: they clear every parameter in Priority 1
Size: they run more than 20 weekly classes
Software: they're on a platform we beat easily

questions.prompt: A drop-in dance studio, set up like a yoga or Pilates studio, hits every parameter: 10 weekly in-person classes, enough bookable staff, owner on LinkedIn, working website. Which code?

options.text: AF1, since it hits every single box
AFH, since it's ready to dial straight away
AFU, since it could be a better fit later on
AF2, since dance is a Priority 2 vertical

questions.reveal: AF1 means the account hits every single box. AF2 means it's slightly off on one, like enough classes but not enough staff. The vertical doesn't change the code.

questions.prompt: A yoga studio opened three months ago and runs 4 weekly classes. The owner posts about adding classes as they grow. What do you do?

options.text: Code it AF2, since it's close enough to dial now
Mark it Dead so it's out of your pool for good
Code it AFU, since it misses now but could fit later
Leave it uncoded, since it doesn't qualify just yet

questions.reveal: AFU isn't a write-off. It marks an account that doesn't fit today, because it misses parameters or runs on software we can't target right now, like ClubReady. Coding it means you can find it again if that changes.
questions.source: Day 3, "Choosing the right code" (AFU as updated)

questions.prompt: Which kind of list updates itself as records meet or stop meeting its criteria?

options.text: A static list
An active list
A sequence
A saved task queue

questions.prompt: On Monday you build a static list of Attempting leads to work all week. By Wednesday, what's the problem?

options.text: Some leads have changed status and no longer belong
It can't be edited, so you can't add new leads
It has doubled in size from new HubSpot imports
Static lists can't be loaded into an Orum session

questions.reveal: Standing views you come back to daily should be active lists. Static lists are for a batch you plan to finish, like today's call list.

questions.prompt: You want to clear out accounts that don't belong in your Book. Which filters fit that job?

options.text: New and Recycled, filtered by vertical and reviews
Attempting, filtered by your code and last activity
Recycled, filtered by past connects and software
Open statuses, filtered for non-ICP vertical or software

questions.source: Day 3, "From Book of Business to a list you can finish" (Job 03)

questions.prompt: You finish pre-vetting and add AF1 to SDR Additional Notes, and nothing else. What's missing?

options.text: Nothing, since the code is what makes it filterable
A task reminding you to dial it tomorrow morning
What you found: who to ask for and what to open with
A static list entry so you can find it again

questions.reveal: The code is how you find the account again. The information is what you say when you get them on the phone, and it pops up in Orum while you dial. A note with one and not the other is half a job.

questions.prompt: Good pre-vetting answers four questions. Which set is right?

options.text: Is it ICP? Is it Priority 1? Is it open? Is it on MindBody?
Worth calling? Who to call? What to know? How to approach?
What vertical? How many classes? How many staff? What software?
Who owns it? What's revenue? How old is it? Who are competitors?

questions.prompt: What's the one question to ask of any piece of research?

options.text: What does this change about how I approach them?
Would the AE want to know this before the demo?
Is this from the business's own website or not?
How long did this take me to find and confirm?

questions.prompt: You've spent 20 minutes on a studio you were always going to call. What's the right move?

options.text: Keep going until you find the owner's mobile
Park it and come back when you have more time
Ask your manager to double-check your research
Write the note with what you have and move on

questions.prompt: While pre-vetting, you find the studio has 12,000 Instagram followers. It doesn't change fit, who you call or your opener. What do you do with it?

options.text: Put it at the top of the note so the AE sees it first
Lead with it as your opener when you get the owner
Leave it out, since it changes nothing about your approach
Code the lead AF1, since that reach signals a strong fit

questions.reveal: If it doesn't change whether you pursue them, who you call or how you open, you didn't need to go looking for it. That's the fastest way to cut research time without losing accuracy.

questions.prompt: A Pilates studio checks every box but one: it's a little short on staff. Everything else is strong. What do you do?

options.text: Mark it Unqualified, since it misses a parameter
Code it AF2 and keep it in your dial rotation
Leave it uncoded until it hires more staff
Pass it to marketing so they can nurture it

questions.reveal: Spend most of your time on the leads that hit every box, but don't sleep on the ones that are slightly off. They still earn dials.
questions.source: Day 4, "Where this usually gets sticky" (filtering too hard); Day 3 codes

questions.prompt: Notes show the owner told another SDR "no" eight months ago. The lead is now Recycled. What do you do?

options.text: Work it, and use that history to shape your opener
Skip it, since she's already turned us down once
Code it AFU so nobody wastes time on it again
Email only, since she clearly didn't want calls

questions.reveal: A past no, to you or to someone else, isn't a reason to give up. The timing may have changed, and now you know what didn't land last time.
questions.source: Day 4, "Where this usually gets sticky" (writing off a past rejection)

questions.prompt: Your manager says your pre-vetting is slow. What's the best change?

options.text: Set a five-minute timer per account and move on when it rings
Skip finding the decision maker and ask for them on the call
Pre-vet only Priority 1 verticals until your speed improves
Know what you're looking for, and stop once the four are answered

questions.prompt: A rep dials straight from an unvetted list to save time. What's most likely to go wrong?

options.text: Booking more meetings than the AEs can take
Running through the whole list before lunch
Reaching the wrong person with nothing to say
Starting a duplicate ownership dispute by accident
